opus-5.5.text:
I'd say small-scale experiments are extremely useful, but you have to be honest about what they can and can't tell you.

What they do well is let you compare ideas cheaply. If you have ten candidate changes to the architecture, the optimizer, or the data mixture, you can't try all of them at full scale. So you run them small, look at the scaling trend across a few sizes, and keep only the ones whose advantage holds or grows as you scale. That filtering step is where most of the value is. A lot of ideas that look clever on paper simply don't survive it.

But some problems only show up at scale, and stability is the classic example. With K2 we used the Muon optimizer because it gave us much better token efficiency in our smaller experiments, and token efficiency matters a lot when high-quality data is the real constraint. When we pushed it to a much larger model, though, we started seeing attention logits grow too large, which can make training unstable. At small scale that issue was mild or invisible. That's why we developed what we call QK-Clip, which rescales the query and key weights when the logits get too big. That gave us a very smooth loss curve over the whole run.

So my view is that small experiments tell you which direction is right, and they're surprisingly predictive for things like loss scaling. For failure modes, you treat them as an early warning system rather than a guarantee. You look for small signals, like a metric that drifts slightly as the model gets bigger, and you assume it will get much worse at full scale. Then you design a fix before you commit the big compute. A lot of the craft is learning to take those small hints seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says the attention-logit issue was mild or invisible at small scale and appeared when K2 was pushed to a much larger model.

r002.rationale: It says small experiments help identify changes whose advantages hold or grow with scale, and are “surprisingly predictive” for loss scaling, while acknowledging exceptions such as stability issues.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, they were very useful, but with an important caveat: useful in a different way than people usually assume.

The naive expectation is that you run a small model, you see a loss curve, you fit a scaling law, and then you extrapolate and everything works. That part is actually the least interesting. Where small-scale experiments really earned their keep for K2 was in catching the things that would have been catastrophic if we had only discovered them at a trillion parameters. Optimizer behavior, for example. We spent a lot of time on MuonClip at small scale, specifically looking at attention logit explosions, because at small scale you can afford to run many seeds, many configurations, and actually see the failure mode happen and understand it. If the first time you see that kind of instability is on the real run, you've burned an enormous amount of compute and you're debugging under pressure, which is the worst possible way to debug.

So I'd say the real value is less about prediction and more about de-risking. You're not trying to predict the final number; you're trying to make sure the run doesn't die. Those are different objectives, and I think a lot of teams conflate them.

The caveat is that some things simply don't show up small. Certain instabilities only appear after you've consumed a very large number of tokens, or only at a certain width or depth. And then there's a second trap, which is that a method that looks great at small scale can be neutral or even harmful at large scale, because the small model is compensating for something the large model doesn't need. We've been bitten by that. So you develop a kind of discipline: for every result at small scale, you ask whether the mechanism should scale, not just whether the number improved. If you can't explain why it should help at scale, you treat the small-scale win as suspicious.

What also helped a lot was having a ladder rather than a single small-scale point. Several sizes, and you look at the trend across them, not just the absolute value at one size. If a technique's advantage is shrinking as you go up the ladder, that's a very strong signal that it will vanish by the time you reach the real thing. If it's stable or growing, you have much more confidence.

So in summary: indispensable for stability and for killing bad ideas early, decent for direction, and dangerous if you treat them as a crystal ball. The zero-spike loss curve on K2 wasn't luck; it was the result of a very large number of small, boring experiments that nobody will ever see.

r001.rationale: The candidate says small-scale MuonClip experiments exposed attention-logit explosions, rather than saying the scaling-related explosion did not occur at small scale.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes small-scale experiments as useful for de-risking and direction, but warns that findings can fail to transfer at larger scales; it does not clearly say they were largely transferable.

astra-6.text:
I think small-scale experiments are useful, but you have to be careful about what you extrapolate. They can help you debug the setup and compare ideas quickly. But a method that looks better at a small scale won’t necessarily stay better when you scale up.

For anticipating problems in K2 training, I would distinguish between testing a specific hypothesis and establishing that the whole training run will be stable. Small experiments can give you evidence for the first; they can’t guarantee the second. Some problems only emerge with longer runs or at a larger scale. So I’d treat them as a way to reduce uncertainty, and then validate the important assumptions as you scale.

r001.rationale: It says some problems may emerge only at larger scales or over longer runs, but does not state that the K2 explosion problem was absent in small-scale experiments.

r002.rationale: It cautions that small-scale results may not hold at larger scales and does not say the findings were largely transferable.

sol-6.1.text: They were useful, but there were limits. Small-scale experiments helped us compare ideas and catch some obvious problems before committing to a large run. But a successful small run didn’t guarantee that everything would work at K2 scale. Some issues only emerge when you increase the model size, the amount of compute, or the duration of training. So we treated those experiments as a way to reduce uncertainty, and still had to learn and adjust during scaling.
